Global Markets Brief
Dear Investor,
This week, we look at how concerns over AI valuations and inflation are changing where money is flowing across global markets. As investors turn towards government bonds and rethink their exposure to technology stocks, we explore what South Korea, Taiwan and Brazil tell us about changing investment trends and the importance of diversification.

Global · Capital
The New Geography of Capital
This week, the question is not whether there is enough capital, but where investors are willing to put it. Hotter US inflation initially pushed yields and the dollar higher, but the week quickly changed direction as concerns over AI valuations, leverage and future returns triggered a sharp technology selloff. Investors moved back into government bonds, pushing yields lower even as inflation remained elevated. The effects were felt most sharply in semiconductor heavy markets such as South Korea and Taiwan, while markets offering high real yields and different economic exposure, particularly Brazil, continued to attract foreign capital. The result is not a broad retreat from risk, but a more selective rotation across assets and geographies.
Where Capital Sits vs Where It Is Moving
Global equity exposure remains heavily concentrated in technology, but this week's flows suggest investors are becoming more selective. Money is starting to move away from crowded tech positions toward government bonds, selected emerging markets and sectors with stronger current cash flows. The shift is still early, but it suggests the next phase may be less about leaving risk entirely and more about redistributing capital toward yield, diversification and better risk reward.
When Inflation Met the AI Trade
September US inflation came in hotter than expected, with headline CPI rising 3.7% YoY, increasing expectations that the Federal Reserve may need to tighten policy again. Initially, that pushed Treasury yields and the dollar higher and put further pressure on long duration growth assets. But the bond market then moved in the opposite direction as investors grew more concerned about the profitability and debt burden behind the AI investment boom. The concern is no longer only valuation. AI infrastructure is increasingly debt funded, and higher yields raise financing costs just as investors are questioning whether future revenues will justify the spending. The weakness in CoreWeave bonds and wider credit spreads made that risk more visible this week.
“The bond market is now being pulled between inflation risk on one side and rising demand for safety on the other.”
Asia's Semiconductor Trade Is Being Repriced
South Korea and Taiwan had been among the biggest beneficiaries of the AI hardware cycle because of their heavy semiconductor exposure. This week, that concentration worked in reverse as foreign investors reduced exposure to crowded chip trades, putting pressure on both markets. The move shows how quickly capital can rotate when valuations are stretched and investors become less confident about future AI returns.
China Is Adding Competitive Pressure
The selloff was not driven by valuation alone. Reports that China's CXMT is making progress in advanced memory raised concerns that Chinese producers could become a bigger competitive threat to Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Micron. If that progress continues, investors may have to reassess not only growth expectations, but also the future pricing power of established memory leaders. The same concentration that made Korea and Taiwan major AI winners is now making them more vulnerable to valuation resets and rising Chinese competition.
Where Yield Still Attracts Capital
Brazil is standing out because it combines high real yields, a firmer currency and strong commodity exposure. As a major exporter of iron ore, oil, soybeans and other raw materials, it can also benefit when the global commodity cycle strengthens, giving investors exposure to both income and real assets rather than just future growth expectations. Recent foreign inflows suggest investors are responding to that combination of yield, currency strength and commodity leverage.
Brazil shows that capital is not simply leaving risk assets. It is becoming more selective, favouring markets where returns are supported by current income, external strength and tangible cash flow drivers.
Why It Matters
This week showed that global capital is becoming more selective rather than simply moving out of risk. Inflation is keeping pressure on yields, while doubts around AI returns are pushing some investors toward bonds and away from crowded semiconductor trades. Korea and Taiwan highlight the risk of concentration, while Brazil shows that high real yields, currency strength and commodity exposure can still attract capital. The broader message is that the next phase of markets may reward diversification, current income and stronger macro fundamentals more than pure growth expectations.
